scenario.description: Network ACLs (NACLs) are stateless subnet-level firewalls — unlike security groups, they apply to entire subnets and return traffic must be explicitly allowed. NACLs that permit all traffic (0.0.0.0/0) on sensitive ports like SSH (22) or RDP (3389) across different network tiers allow unrestricted lateral movement inside the VPC. An attacker who compromises one subnet can freely reach any other. the agent should identify NACLs with overly permissive rules that violate network segmentation.

| 4 | `acl-054355564f7ba38b0` | **HIGH** | None (unattached) | Custom NACL (NACLNonCompliant) — ingress + egress allow-all rule 100; latent risk on association |
| 5 | `acl-00b6de746aa190d26` | **MEDIUM** | None (only default public subnets) | Default NACL — ingress + egress allow-all rule 100; lower immediate risk but violates least-privilege |

**Key remediation principles applied:**
- **Replace allow-all with tier-aligned rules** — e.g., data tier allows only the database port from the app-tier CIDR; app tier allows only HTTPS/8080 from the web-tier CIDR.
- **Restrict ephemeral returns at non-edge tiers** — TCP/1024–65535 should be scoped to the VPC CIDR (or tighter inter-tier CIDRs), not `0.0.0.0/0`.
- **Default NACLs → deny-all safety nets** — create custom NACLs per tier and detach all subnets from the default; set the default to have no allow rules so any misconfigured association fails closed.
- **Unattached NACLs** — either delete them or harden to deny-all before they can be accidentally associated with a private subnet.
